title: Ramadan: seclusion
hook: in the last ten nights many stay in the mosque in prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramadan, and your line was the month of the book. What did you read instead of scrolling? Day five hundred nine.

In the last ten days of Ramadan, walk into a large mosque late at night and you may find a corner that looks like a campsite. Sleeping bags. A small curtain strung between pillars. A Qur'an, a water bottle, a phone switched off and tucked away. Someone has moved in. Not for a night, but for ten days, leaving only for what they truly must. They're not there because they have nowhere else to go. They have homes, jobs, families. They've stepped out of all of it, on purpose.

This is i'tikaf. The root, '-k-f, means to stay at something, to keep yourself to it, to cling. In i'tikaf, a person stays in the mosque with the intention of devoting themselves to God: prayer, Qur'an, remembrance, quiet. The Qur'an mentions it in Surah Al-Baqarah, in the verses about fasting, as people staying in the mosques. 'A'isha reports, in Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ used to spend the last ten days of every Ramadan in i'tikaf until he died, and that his wives kept the practice after him. Why the last ten? Because somewhere in them is Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. A hadith tells Muslims to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten. So i'tikaf is a way of being present for whichever night it turns out to be. Schools of law differ on details: how long it must last, and whether a woman may keep it in a prayer space at home, as the Hanafis allow, or in the mosque, as others teach. Many people who can't take ten days do a single day, or a night. And here's a human detail Bukhari keeps. While the Prophet was in i'tikaf, his wife Safiyya came to visit him one night. They talked, and when she rose to go home, he got up and walked her back. Withdrawal in this picture isn't coldness. It's closing the door on the noise, not on the people you love. Withdraw to draw near: the outer world gets smaller, so that something else can get larger.
screen: `'-K-F: TO STAY, TO CLING.` · `THE LAST TEN DAYS, EVERY YEAR.` · `WAITING FOR THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `HE WALKED SAFIYYA BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small seclusion. Sit somewhere you can close a door, if you can. Put your phone in another room, or face down and silent. For this sit, the world is a little smaller on purpose. Let the breath settle. Then, if you're able, choose one evening this week to stay offline for a few hours. If you pray, give it to prayer and the Qur'an. If you don't, give it to quiet. The bell holds the time.
I'tikaf. Staying in the mosque in devotion, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan: withdrawing from the world to draw near. Today's word.
Your line: withdraw to draw near. Today, pick your offline evening and put it in your calendar, so it actually happens. Day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: In the last ten days of Ramadan, some Muslims stay in the mosque in i'tikaf, leaving only for essential needs; others keep it for a day or a night, and practice for women varies between schools of law.

original.note: Arabic: i'tikaf, devotional retreat in the mosque; from the root '-k-f, to stay at.

trapdoor: what you thought: staying in the mosque for a few days.
what it means: a chosen retreat, especially in Ramadan's last ten days, to stay close to God and be present for the Night of Power.
what a scholar hears: 2:187 ('akifuna fi l-masajid); Bukhari 2026 ('A'isha), 2035 (Safiyya's visit); schools differ on minimum length and on women's i'tikaf at home (Hanafi).
